items.speaker: Ray Dalio
items.occasion: Bloomberg Television interview
items.quote: If there’s not a high enough real return, those bonds are not appreciated.
items.summary: Dalio said US debt is past the point of no return, that the bond market already shows early signs of a debt crisis (long rates rising versus short rates, weaker dollar, flows into gold), and that the resulting stagflation leaves the Fed in a very difficult position with Chair Warsh facing a test from the bond market. He said the path is heading toward 1930s-style financial repression. He also said equity bubble gauges are close to 1929 and 2000 levels and that all great technology changes produce bubbles.
items.score_note: Two-sided: investors need a higher real return now, but he expects eventual yield suppression by the central bank. No direct statement on the next rate move, so scored at 0.

items.speaker: David Solomon
items.occasion: Goldman Sachs Q2 2026 earnings call
items.quote: The build-out of AI infrastructure remains in its early stages.
items.summary: No comment on the Fed rate path. Solomon said the AI investment cycle is widening capital needs into infrastructure, energy and data centers, that this multi-year cycle will keep financing and capital formation elevated, that leveraged finance activity is partly tied to the AI build, and that Goldman raised $31 billion in private credit in the quarter.
items.score_note: AI-financing and private-credit content only. Quote is in the transcript data embedded in the Fortune/Quartr page (script block).

items.quote: The only point we're always trying to make is when there's a credit cycle, and there will be a credit cycle, how will everybody perform?
items.summary: No comment on the Fed rate path. Dimon said the weakening in credit underwriting standards is 'a very mild one' but spread across several dimensions (revenue assumptions, expense add-backs, more PIK, weaker covenants, rollover/interest-rate risk) and concentrated in some players. He also said AI capex went from about $400 billion to $700 billion and that global deficits of 4.5-5% are competing for the same capital.
items.score_note: No statement about what the Fed will or should do. The quote sits in the transcript data embedded in the Fortune/Quartr page (inside a script block), not in the visible article text.

items.speaker: Jamie Dimon
items.occasion: Master Investor Podcast with Wilfred Frost (recorded July 16, released July 20)
items.quote: even if inflation was 2%, the 10-year bond should probably be at 4.5% to 4%, and the short rate should be 3.25% to 3.5%
items.summary: Dimon said he would not buy long-dated Treasuries and would not give the latest good inflation print much credence. He put the appropriate short rate at 3.25-3.5% even with inflation at 2%, adding that rates are almost there today, and warned that debt and deficits will show up as higher interest rates and a rattled market.
items.score_note: He gives a level for where the short rate should be at 2% inflation and says policy is only about there while he distrusts the disinflation data, which implies policy is not restrictive. No explicit call for a hike, so +1 not +2. Date is the release date per Quartz (recorded July 16).

items.occasion: CNBC 'Closing Bell' interview after the July FOMC hold
items.quote: If you really want to get to 2%, I think you have to raise interest rates
items.summary: After the Fed held at 3.50-3.75% with three dissents for a hike, Gundlach said reaching 2% inflation requires raising rates and may not happen for a couple of years. He read the long-bond selloff during the press conference as bond vigilantes telling the Fed to back its rhetoric with action.
items.score_note: Says rates have to go up to reach the inflation target. CNBC's July 30 follow-up from the same interview carries his comment that corporate credit is softening with AI and tech spreads moving wider.

On private credit he walked through a fund markdown from 100 to 81, said some holdings must be worth close to zero, and described AI bond deals plus passive inflows as a dumping ground for overvalued IPOs.

items.summary: Dalio agreed that markets show classic signs of a bubble and, per Fortune's paraphrase, named two forces that typically prick one: rising interest rates that make debt costlier to service and a surge in stock issuance. No statement about what the Fed will or should do.
items.score_note: Bubble and issuance commentary only. Podcast recording date not given on the page, so the article date is used.

items.speaker: Jamie Dimon
items.occasion: CNBC 'Closing Bell: Overtime' interview with Leslie Picker, Los Angeles
items.quote: If there's inflation, they will have to fight it.
items.summary: Asked whether the long-end selloff is a credibility test for the Fed, Dimon said the real question is whether there is inflation, noted it has been over 3% for five years, and said the Fed will have to fight it if it persists. He backed Chair Warsh's review of inflation measurement and the balance sheet and dismissed complaints about the end of forward guidance. On credit he said market leverage (margin, prime broker, hedge fund) is high but not systemic, he is not worried about private credit systemically, and hyperscaler data-center spending will 'ultimately play out and pay out' though individual data-center projects need deal-by-deal analysis.
items.score_note: Conditional statement that the Fed will have to fight inflation, paired with his view that the odds favor higher inflation and rates. Leans tighter but no call for an immediate hike.
items.ai_quote: So, in my own view, and I may be wrong, it'll ultimately play out and pay out.

items.speaker: Ray Dalio
items.occasion: LinkedIn post on the Treasury buyback expansion and the US debt path
items.quote: it would be very bad if the Federal Reserve unnaturally forced interest rates down
items.summary: Dalio wrote that the government's finances are at an inflection point after Treasury's buyback move and that a debt crisis could arrive in about three years, give or take two. His fix needs spending cuts, higher tax revenue and lower interest rates at the same time, but he warned against the Fed forcing rates down. He advised being underweight bonds and holding gold.
items.score_note: He says lower rates are part of the solution but that the Fed must not push them down artificially; the two points offset, so 0. LinkedIn original not opened; quotes from CNBC.

items.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
items.role: Chairman and CEO, Duquesne Family Office
items.occasion: Wall Street Journal op-ed 'Let the Bond Market Speak'
items.quote: Then do the only thing that durably lowers long-term yields: address the primary deficit.
items.summary: Druckenmiller argued that Treasury's doubled long-dated buybacks are price management, that a 30-year yield of 5.5% would be 'an invoice' not a crisis, and that governments defending prices against fundamentals always lose. The piece is aimed at Treasury and fiscal policy; the quoted passages do not say what the Fed should do with the policy rate.
items.score_note: Statement about Treasury buybacks and long yields, no usable view on the Fed rate path in the text read. WSJ original is paywalled; quotes taken from CNBC's report.

items.speaker: David Solomon
items.occasion: CNBC interview with Sara Eisen at the G20 finance meeting, Asheville
items.quote: I won't speculate on Fed rate decisions.
items.summary: Asked whether raising rates now would be right, Solomon declined to speculate, saying only that Chair Warsh is focused on inflation while data-dependent and that policy rates and the long-term premium follow different dynamics. He said a 5% long yield is not a calamity and reflects fundamentals. On debt-financed AI capex he said it bears monitoring but he sees no systemic risk now because most issuance comes from large companies with strong cash flow, though some areas will overextend and need recalibration.
items.score_note: He explicitly declines to give a view on the Fed. Goldman's page is dated Sept 3 and states the interview was recorded Aug 31.
items.ai_quote: Over time, it is something to monitor: the total size of the investment and how much of it is debt-financed.

items.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
items.role: Chairman and CEO, Duquesne Family Office
items.occasion: Private remarks at a Piper Sandler investor event in New York, reported by the Financial Times
items.quote: Committee members on the Fed who keep saying Fed fund rates are restrictive are just ridiculous
items.summary: According to FT-based reports, Druckenmiller told a closed-door audience that US borrowing costs remain a little low, that rate cuts are no longer needed, and that officials who call the funds rate restrictive are ridiculous given asset prices worldwide. He called Warsh a great Fed chair and said he is no longer allowed to speak with him.
items.score_note: Says policy is not restrictive and yields are too low, which pushes back on easing; no explicit call for hikes in the quoted text. Secondary source (Yahoo/TheStreet citing Investing.com and the FT); the FT original was not opened. Event date Sept 10 per PrimeXBT and Newsquawk reports of the same remarks.

items.speaker: Jamie Dimon
items.occasion: Yahoo Finance interview after the September FOMC hike
items.quote: It's not clear to me we've slayed inflation
items.summary: Hours after the Fed raised rates, Dimon said he is not convinced inflation is beaten and that every business should be prepared for volatility in interest rates. Per Yahoo he said persistent inflation, global deficits and heavy capital demand, including for AI, could keep upward pressure on rates, while low unemployment and corporate profits show the economy is not near a downturn; rising unemployment is what would bring consumer and corporate credit losses.
items.score_note: Sees the inflation fight as unfinished and rates biased higher, without calling for a specific further hike.

items.quote: I would have just done the 50 and then see what the data does

He called Warsh's press conference thin and opaque and criticized the Fed task forces. DoubleLine's recap adds that AI-related investment-grade bonds have widened about 50bp while the rest of IG barely moved.

items.speaker: Howard Marks
items.occasion: Oaktree memo 'Shall We Repeal the Laws of Economics - Part III'
items.quote: arguing against the likelihood of a decline in interest rates anytime soon
items.summary: Marks argued that long-term yields reflect fundamentals (inflation well above target, which is why the Fed hiked the prior week, no fiscal discipline, and heavy capital demand from the AI buildout) and that Treasury buybacks treat the symptom. He wrote that the goal should not be to get interest rates down but to address what is pushing them up, and that net Treasury issuance plus AI capital needs argue against lower rates soon.
items.score_note: Forecast that rates will not fall soon and endorsement of the reasons for the September hike; mostly about long yields, no call on the next FOMC move. credit_view left null because he treats AI financing only as a source of capital demand, not as a credit-quality judgment.

items.summary: Dalio said interest rates can still rise without sinking equities because earnings growth provides a cushion, but that cushion is shrinking and credit spreads are starting to widen. items.quote: I have always thought there is a higher chance than other people.

He said JPMorgan is tightening up on credit because terms have become a little loose, and that shrinking the Fed balance sheet will require changes (to liquidity rules). items.occasion: Post on X ahead of the December FOMC
items.quote: The Fed will put the U.S. and world in recession if it continues to raise rates in a failed attempt to drive inflation to 2%
items.summary: Ackman said the Fed is about to make another mistake on December 9 if it hikes into sharply tighter financial conditions, noting a higher cost of equity and that SpaceX recently paid over 8% on secured debt. He called the 2% target misguided and 3% more realistic given military spending, de-globalization, tariffs and the AI infrastructure and energy buildout.
items.score_note: Opposes a December hike and further tightening. 'Another mistake' implies the September hike was one, which would fit -2, but he does not ask for cuts, so the level nearer 0 is used. X post not opened; the page gives no post date, so the article date is used.
items.ai_quote: the massive AI infrastructure and related energy investment are features of the world that did not exist when the 2% target was set

coverage_notes: David Tepper: searched CNBC, Yahoo, Stocktwits, Fortune and general web; no public statement on the Fed, rates or credit found in the window (only 13F coverage), so zero items. Paul Tudor Jones: only the Oct 13 CNBC Squawk Box interview found in the window (his 'no chance Warsh cuts' interview was May 7, outside it); no full transcript located, so the item rests on CNBC's live blog and Oct 30 recap. Druckenmiller: nothing found for June, July or October; the Aug 24 WSJ op-ed and the Sept 10 Piper Sandler remarks (FT) are paywalled, so both rest on secondary reports with direct quotes. Dimon: June has no item (the Council on Foreign Relations remarks reported June 15-21 were about the bull market and geopolitics, with no Fed or credit content); November has no new statement found. Dalio: no item for July, September or November; LinkedIn originals (Aug 21, Oct 13) were not opened, quotes come from CNBC and Stocktwits. Gundlach: four occasions (June 9 and Sept 8 webcasts, June 15 Zulauf talk, June 17 CNBC) are in 'unverified' because DoubleLine's pages paraphrase him without a direct quote; nothing found for November. Ken Griffin: one item (Oct 20); Citadel Securities' own transcript page and the Bloomberg video did not load. El-Erian: his X posts and Bloomberg/FT columns were not opened; two interview items only. Bloomberg, FT, WSJ, Business Insider, Advisor Perspectives, Moneywise and thewealthadvisor.com pages were blocked or paywalled. Method notes: (1) earnings-call items cite Fortune's Quartr-powered transcript pages, where the transcript text sits in embedded page data (a script block), so a substring check must run on the raw HTML rather than visible text; (2) an extra field 'ai_quote_url' is filled when the ai_quote comes from a different page than source_url (null means same page); (3) 'credit_view' added per assignment. Context check: pages opened agree with the brief (September 25bp hike to 3.75-4.00%, October hold, December hike priced); CNBC additionally reports three dissents in favor of a hike at the July meeting and Fortune/Stocktwits put December hike odds near 93% on Nov 22.
